node.label: Harold A. Innis
node.date_label: The Fur Trade in Canada 1930 · The Cod Fisheries 1940 · Empire and Communications 1950 · The Bias of Communication 1951 · coverage through 2000
node.description: A Toronto political economist whose staple studies read Canada's development through the export of raw materials to industrial centres in Britain and the United States. The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) concludes that 'the economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization', that the history of the fur trade is 'the history of contact between two civilizations', and that 'the present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it'. The Cod Fisheries (1940) follows a second staple as the history of an international economy. After 1940 he turned to the media of communication and empire (Empire and Communications, 1950; The Bias of Communication, 1951).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Harold A. Innis (1894–1952); The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (1930); The Cod Fisheries: The History of an International Economy (1940); Empire and Communications (1950); The Bias of Communication (1951; 1964 reissue with an introduction by Marshall McLuhan). Readings: Brady's memoir (1953); Watkins, “A Staple Theory of Economic Growth” (1963); Salmon (1997).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the staple studies. The Fur Trade in Canada is checked at its contents and its conclusion (pp. 386–397, read in a scan of the 1930 edition); The Cod Fisheries and the two communication books are checked at catalogue level, and the turn to communication rests on Brady's 1953 memoir. He is not presented as the originator of the staple approach. Watkins (1963) calls him its 'leading innovator' but adds that 'others tilled the same vineyard'. Salmon (1997) notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory', Brady names Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies', and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the fur-trade book. The 1930 conclusion's statements about Indigenous peoples (their 'limited cultural background'; that Canada 'has had no serious problems with her native peoples') are recorded as claims of 1930, not adopted. The atlas has no communication-studies entry; the McLuhan introduction is noted from the catalogue only.

proposed_edges.relationship: The staple studies: Canada read through its exports of fur and fish (1930, 1940)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Innis's own statement, 1930 conclusion (pp. 386–397 read): 'The economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization. Energy has been directed toward the exploitation of staple products and the tendency has been cumulative' (p. 388); 'The northern half of North America remained British because of the importance of fur as a staple product' (p. 396); 'The present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it' (p. 397). Watkins (1963, opening paragraphs read) calls him 'the leading innovator' whose work 'stamped the “school”', with an approach 'more technological history writ large than a theory of economic growth'. Brady (1953, read in full) traces his study of 'the staple industries, beginning with the fur trade and fisheries' (p. 89). Salmon (1997, pp. 180–181 read): the staple thesis 'provided an economic rationale for Canadian political development'. A contribution, not a founding: Watkins says 'others tilled the same vineyard', Salmon notes that 'Innis never claimed to have originated the staples theory' (n. 2), Brady calls Adam Shortt 'the pioneer in these economic studies' (p. 91), and Mackintosh's 1923 article precedes the book. The Cod Fisheries is checked at catalogue level only. In the sampled corpus, 82 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite any of his works; the citation share falls from 7.1% (2009–14) and 6.8% (2015–19) to 4.9% (2020–26). Of the 82, 48 cite The Fur Trade in Canada and 6 The Cod Fisheries. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The staples strand names Innis with Mackintosh, Lower and Watkins and cites the same two books and Watkins's opening; the evidence fits it exactly. The Laurentian strand (Creighton's expansion of Innis's thesis, via Salmon) is Creighton's contribution, not Innis's, so it is not targeted.

proposed_edges.relationship: The fur trade as economic history, a resource later reworked with Indigenous traders as actors
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Innis's 1930 conclusion (pp. 392, 397 read) calls the history of the fur trade 'the history of contact between two civilizations, the European and the North American', and writes: 'We have not yet realized that the Indian and his culture were fundamental to the growth of Canadian institutions.' Brady (1953, p. 90) lists among the book's themes 'the relation between the culture of the Indian and the spread of European power' and 'the adaptation of the Indian to the needs of the trade'. Salmon's 1979 review of Ray and Freeman's 'Give Us Good Measure' (1978), read in full, says they 'have presented the Indians of the fur trade as “economic man”' from the Hudson's Bay Company account books, which 'Harold Innis was unable to use', and that 'the authors do continue the Innis tradition of innovative research'. That is a reviewer's characterisation: how Ray and Freeman discuss Innis, and Eccles's 1979 'belated review' of the book, are unread. A resource, not a founder: the roster keeps Innis as a precursor, and the 1930 conclusion's characterisations of Indigenous peoples are not adopted. In the sampled corpus, 48 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite The Fur Trade in Canada; of the 44 assigned a home field, 23 fall in the 'Indigenous peoples, fur trade & the West' co-citation cluster. Of the 72 fielded dissertations citing any of his works, 39% fall there, 2.8 times that cluster's base rate. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Salmon's review connects Innis to Ray's line of work, and Ray (1974) anchors indigenous_actors_in_trade. Ray and Freeman 1978 is not registered in the atlas; nnreq_ray_1974 is cited only to identify the strand. The alternative, fur_trade_national_economy, is Innis's own strand, so an arrow there would point at himself. edge_870 (cdn_national_tradition — native_newcomer comparison) stays: it compares the two fields' shared subject, while this arrow is the person's directed contribution.
proposed_edges.include_note: Excluded by Claude, 2026-10-13: rests on a reviewer's characterization (Salmon 1979) rather than Ray's own text; the same gap Sol flagged for the Innis–Ray edge in 1.128.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Checked evidence exists but would duplicate edge_797 (cdn_national_tradition → economic: the staple approach as a Canadian contribution to economic history, citing Watkins's 'leading innovator'). Brady (1953, p. 90) says The Fur Trade in Canada 'established the reputation of its author as one of the leading economic historians in North America', and p. 95 records his presidency of the Economic History Association (1942); these are reputation and office, not a distinct contribution to one of the economic entry's strands. Two arrows should not tell the same story. If reviewers prefer a person-level arrow, edge_797 would need relabelling first, as edge_886 was for Thompson.

No checked evidence. Brady (pp. 88–89) records the influence on him of Veblen, J. M. Clark's overhead costs and C. S. Duncan's marketing lectures at Chicago, none of whom anchors the Historical economics entry (German and British historical economics before 1920).

The atlas has no communication or media entry to target. Brady (pp. 91–92, 94–95) checks the turn to 'the media of communication' and calls Empire and Communications a book that 'served a purpose in setting forth a theme for future social scientists to pursue'; McLuhan's 1964 introduction is catalogue-level only. In the sampled corpus 8 of the 82 citing dissertations cite one of the two communication books.

new_sources.title: Harold A. Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (New Haven: Yale University Press; London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1930), contents and chapter VI, “Conclusion”, pp. 386–397.
new_sources.citation: Harold A. Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1930), ch. VI, “Conclusion”, pp. 386–397.

verification.note: Read in two independent scans of the 1930 Yale edition on the Internet Archive (furtradeincanada0000haro; FURTRADEINCANADA, University of Victoria Libraries copy); their OCR texts agree at the quoted passages. Title page (Yale University Press and Humphrey Milford, 1930; preface by R. M. MacIver), author's preface (dated June 1929), contents and conclusion pp. 386–397 read. Contents: VI. Conclusion: 1. The Importance of Staple Products (386); 2. The Fur Trade (389); 3. The Forest Industries (397); 4. Capitalism and the Staples (401). Quoted: 'The economic history of Canada has been dominated by the discrepancy between the center and the margin of western civilization. Energy has been directed toward the exploitation of staple products and the tendency has been cumulative' (p. 388); 'The history of the fur trade is the history of contact between two civilizations, the European and the North American' and 'The limited cultural background of the North American hunting peoples' (p. 392); 'The northern half of North America remained British because of the importance of fur as a staple product' and 'The Northwest Company was the forerunner of the present confederation' (p. 396); 'Canada has had no serious problems with her native peoples since the fur trade depended primarily on these races', 'We have not yet realized that the Indian and his culture were fundamental to the growth of Canadian institutions' and 'The present Dominion emerged not in spite of geography but because of it' (p. 397). Chapters II–V and pp. 398–410 not read.

new_sources.scope_note: Innis's own 1930 statement of the staple argument and of the fur trade as contact between civilizations.

new_sources.title: Alexander Brady, "Harold Adams Innis, 1894–1952," Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science 19, no. 1 (1953): 87–96.
new_sources.citation: Alexander Brady, "Harold Adams Innis, 1894–1952," Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science 19, no. 1 (February 1953): 87–96.

verification.note: Read in full (Cambridge Core PDF; Crossref: CJEPS 19:1, Feb. 1953, pp. 87–96). Born 5 November 1894 near Otterville, died 8 November 1952 (p. 87); Veblen, Clark and Duncan as Chicago influences (pp. 88–89); study of 'the staple industries, beginning with the fur trade and fisheries' (p. 89); The Fur Trade in Canada as 'his first notable achievement in economic interpretation', with themes including 'the relation between the culture of the Indian and the spread of European power' and 'the adaptation of the Indian to the needs of the trade'; 'modern Canada had emerged, not in spite of geography, but because of it'; it 'established the reputation of its author as one of the leading economic historians in North America' (p. 90); 'Adam Shortt, as Innis would promptly admit, was the pioneer in these economic studies' (p. 91); 'after 1940 he became increasingly absorbed by the wider themes of cultural history' and 'more keenly interested in the media of communication' (pp. 91–92); Empire and Communications (1950; the 1948 Beit Lectures) 'served a purpose in setting forth a theme for future social scientists to pursue' (pp. 94–95); president of the Economic History Association, 1942 (p. 95). A colleague's memorial, not a critical assessment.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period memoir: the staple studies, the turn to communication, and Shortt as the earlier pioneer.

new_sources.title: M. Stephen Salmon, review of Arthur J. Ray and Donald B. Freeman, "Give Us Good Measure": An Economic Analysis of Relations Between the Indians and the Hudson's Bay Company Before 1763 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1978), Archivaria 8 (Summer 1979): 186–187.
new_sources.citation: M. Stephen Salmon, review of Ray and Freeman, "Give Us Good Measure" (1978), Archivaria 8 (Summer 1979): 186–187.

verification.note: Review read in full (Archivaria PDF; journal metadata: vol. 8, Summer 1979, pp. 186–187, book-review section). Ray and Freeman 'have presented the Indians of the fur trade as “economic man”'; their 'major contribution to the history of the fur trade is their detailed examination of the Hudson's Bay Company's account books' (p. 186); 'While it is sobering to remember that Harold Innis was unable to use the records of the Hudson's Bay Company, the authors do continue the Innis tradition of innovative research' (p. 187). The book under review is unread; its own discussion of fur-trade historiography (part one) is not checked. Ray and Freeman 1978 matches Open Library work OL2175957W (UTP, 1978).

new_sources.scope_note: A 1979 reviewer places Ray and Freeman's economic analysis of Indian–HBC trade in 'the Innis tradition'.
